articles.title: Distraction-free writing gadget BYOK is adding custom extensions
articles.summary: BYOK’s solution for adding features to its distraction-free writing tool without bloat is an optional scripting system.
articles.body: BYOK is a no-frills, single-purpose gadget that 90 percent of people will find absolutely frivolous. But for those who spend a significant chunk of their lives putting words to virtual paper, there is an obvious allure. Personally, I think it’s at its best when you just stick to the bare minimum, focusing on pure text drafting. Certain users, though, need more. They want BYOK to take notes, they want to use it for writing screenplays, or maybe they want to organize a sprawling novel. Balancing the wants and needs of these more demanding users has been a challenge that BYOK founder Nick Sjolinder has been trying to figure out how to tackle. The answer he seems to have landed on, is scripts. Rather than clutter BYOK with a ton of features that 80 percent of its users wont touch, or crowd the Studio app with even more formats, the company is planning to implement optional scripts that expand the capabilities of BYOK. [Media: A few examples of the kinds of thing people will be able to create are a screenplay assistant, a character note tool, and a writing analyzer. This could let users highlight text in a document and pull it out as a note or tell them when they’re using the passive voice. It’s still early in development and the scripting features haven’t rolled out publicly, but BYOK is asking for feedback from its users.

articles.title: China’s robots race ahead
articles.summary: Bots were breaking records and breaking down at Beijing’s World Humanoid Robot Games.
articles.body: This is The Stepback, a weekly newsletter breaking down one essential story from the tech world. For more on falling robots and the US-China AI race, follow Robert Hart. The Stepback arrives in our subscribers’ inboxes on Sunday at 8AM ET. Opt in for The Stepback here. How it started I’ve admitted my fondness for robot fail videos on Stepback before, and let me tell you the World Humanoid Robot Games did not disappoint. [Media: The five-day event, which wrapped this week in Beijing, brought high drama, and brought it well. One robot, made by smartphone maker Honor, lost a leg mid-sprint, while others tripped in a flurry of sparks. Another finisher ran straight into a crash mat, bounced off it, and promptly burst into flames. In the weightlifting, one robot lost its balance beneath a modest barbell and toppled inexorably into the judges’ table, arms cartoonishly aloft. Robotic cheerleaders tumbled and stumbled through routines, while a separate bot fell off a platform in circumstances that, had it been human, might have looked suspiciously like it was gawking at the performers. [Media: This was only the second World Humanoid Robot Games, though it was already far bigger than the inaugural event last year. Unlike this year, last year’s records were paltry. The winning 100-meter sprint was a glacial 21.50 seconds and the highest standing high jump was just 0.95 meters. In keeping with China’s habit of turning robots into public spectacle — from intricate dances at a Spring Festival Gala to demos at major tech events — both this and last year’s games were staged in Beijing’s National Speed Skating Oval, a former Olympic venue. And a spectacle it was. At most sporting events, contestants losing limbs, careening into walls, catching fire, and regularly being carried away on stretchers — oh, and did I mention catching fire?! — would probably be grounds to stop proceedings. At the Humanoid Robot Games, it was par for the course. Fire aside, the games were unusual in other ways too. Alongside familiar events like sprinting, football, boxing, and weightlifting were more unusual competitions in bed-making, parcel delivery, shelf stacking, clothes folding, and hammering nails. Aptly, there was a firefighting contest too. These less standard offerings spoke to the real purpose of the games: getting robots out of the lab and into the messy real-world environments their makers hope they will ultimately work in. And China is making no secret of wanting to lead the way. How it’s going For all the spectacle and drama, the games show there has been massive progress in robotics in recent years. Records fell, with one humanoid running the 100-meter sprint in 9.39 seconds, beating Usain Bolt’s 2009 world record. Another bot reached 2.88 meters in a standing high jump, nearly half a meter above the human high-jump record that has stood since 1993. Those performances are almost unrecognizable compared to robotics competitions a decade ago, when even the most advanced machines struggled to stay upright. But the games also show how far there is to go before humanoids are actually useful in the real world. The flashy, video-friendly sporting events were impressive, but the more mundane tasks were less thrilling — I don’t see picking up soybeans with tweezers, block-building, or powder-weighing becoming Olympic mainstays anytime soon. While many events required robots to operate autonomously — including gymnastics, football, tug of war, table tennis, and some track events — others allowed for human assistance via teleoperation, albeit with a scoring penalty. The dexterity being displayed certainly points to genuine and impressive hardware improvements, but seems like there is still a long way to go before these machines can operate reliably on their own in places like factories or homes. What happens next Beijing has not yet confirmed a third Humanoid Robot Games, but given the government’s enthusiasm for the industry, it would be surprising to not get another installment. The city has already confirmed another humanoid half-marathon for April, and the country plans to open its first robot-run hotel next year. China was the undisputed champion of the games, and the country looks well placed to stay in top position moving forward — both at future competitions and in the humanoid robot industry as a whole. The medal table was almost entirely a Chinese affair, dominated in particular by AgiBot and Tien Kung, each scooping up more medals than nearly every other competitor combined, excluding the other. In part, that asymmetry reflected the lack of international competition. Although the games were framed as a global affair, 641 of 666 teams were Chinese, domestically representing 157 companies and 200 universities, according to state-run China Daily. While there doesn’t seem to be a public breakdown of entrants, the biggest US humanoid players like Tesla, Boston Dynamics, and Figure were conspicuous by their absence. Nevertheless, the sheer diversity of Chinese institutions represented in Beijing was a show of force, and a sign of how quickly the country’s robotics sector is maturing, even amid growing concerns about circular investment, thriving companies that lack viable products, and a possible humanoid bubble. It’s not clear a stronger US showing at the games would’ve changed much. The US still has an edge in frontier AI and advanced chips, but China has been rapidly closing parts of that gap, while also making embodied AI a strategic national priority. The same cannot be said of Washington, which has for years paid much less attention to robotics and now trails China in nearly every regard, including manufacturing, deployment, and hardware. Some reports even suggest that recent efforts to ban foreign robots, a general policy squarely aimed at China, could backfire, given how dependent domestic firms are on Chinese components. Catching up to China will take serious and concerted effort, but given how quickly the technology is moving, there’s still time to make up ground. Washington is already treating other areas of AI as strategic priorities in its competition with Beijing; robotics could be one of them. There will be plenty of stumbling along the way, and, hopefully, plenty more robot fail videos too. By the way * DARPA still runs robotics challenges, but they drew far more attention a decade ago. * When the US government banned foreign robots, it didn’t just ban humanoids and quadrupeds. It banned Roombas too, reports The Verge’s own Sean Hollister. * “The brains may come from the US, but the body could very well be Made In China,” writes Business Insider’s Lloyd Lee in a report setting out how the US could do with bolstering its hardware supply chain. * Unlike language models, you can’t simply scrape the internet to build an AI capable of interacting with the real world. A lot of that data has to be generated, which is why companies desperately want to film you doing chores, or send someone to your house to film them doing them. Read this * The Atlantic and the South China Morning Post both have great sets of pictures showing highlights of the games worth checking out. * Why do we keep laughing when robots fail? An old but still good exploration of that shared joy in vintage Vice. * You can learn a lot about a robot by kicking it, says Verge alum James Vincent in an excellent Harper’s feature outlining the state of play in the humanoid industry. * I’m not only about robot fail videos. I can hate them in real life too, as I did with Casio’s fluffy AI pet thing, Moflin.

articles.title: Two new small, powerful Macs
articles.summary: Plus: a new Star Wars game, a Nokia phone that can charge your phone, a Wyze cam with a great privacy feature, and more.
articles.body: Hi, friends! Welcome to Installer No. 142, your guide to the best and Verge-iest stuff in the world. (If you’re new here, welcome, how is it almost September already, and also you can read all the old editions at the Installer homepage.) This week, I’ve been remembering Dolly Parton, Tim Curry, and Peter Cullen, absorbing everything in Rockstar’s big GTA VI preview, wondering if Apple will announce a foldable iPhone at its September event, getting sucked into Summoning Salt’s latest speedrunning documentary about competitive Tetris, listening to Weird Al’s new Tiny Desk concert (“The Saga Begins!”), and getting a Reuben from my favorite local spot after thinking about it for months. This week, I also have for you new Macs, a Nokia phone that can charge your phone, a Wyze cam with a great privacy feature, and more. Programming note: Installer is off next week. I’ll be on vacation. See you next month for Techtember! (As always, the best part of Installer is your ideas and tips. What do you want to know more about? What are your favorite things you’ve watched / seen / listened to / eaten recently? Drop a line to installer@theverge.com. And if you know someone else who might enjoy Installer, forward it to them and tell them to subscribe here.) The Drop * The M6 and M5 Pro Mac Mini. Apple updated its tiny computer this week, and you can preorder it with a new M6 chip or an M5 Pro. Unfortunately, they have starting prices that are $100 more expensive than the previous generation, and the new model won’t be released until September 22nd. The company also refreshed the Mac Studio, and you can preorder it with a new M5 Ultra chip. * Star Wars: Zero Company. This strategy game set in the Star Wars universe has been getting rave reviews. Gotta find some time to squeeze this in with all of the other big games coming out soon. * HMD’s Nokia 300 Charge. HMD made an old-school, candybar-style Nokia dumbphone that doubles as a power bank. It also has a 3.5mm headphone jack. Who needs a foldable iPhone when you can have this? * Wyze’s Indoor Cam Pan. This new $39.98 security camera can tilt 360 degrees around and 103 degrees vertically, but it also has a privacy mode that tilts the lens fully downward into the body of the camera so that it can’t see anything. Great feature. * Garmin’s Fenix 9 smartwatches. The Fenix 9 and 9 Pro have OLED screens, 64GB of storage, and for the two bigger sizes of the 9 Pro, the option to get solar-charging displays. The watches aren’t cheap, though: The Fenix 9 starts at $999.99, while the Pro starts at $1,099.99. * Elden Ring: Tarnished Edition. The Switch 2 version of FromSoftware’s all-time classic is apparently worth the wait after a big delay. Do I need yet another excuse to get lost in The Lands Between? Probably not, but I’m tempted. * Whoop’s Meridian Band. This $149 band is made from Milanese mesh, comes in gold, rose gold, silver, and black, and makes your fifth-gen Whoop tracker look super fancy. But one part isn’t so fancy: You can’t charge your Whoop while it’s in the Meridian Band. Screen Share Today I’m featuring John Gruber of Daring Fireball. If you follow Apple and are a regular Verge reader (which, as an Installer subscriber, I assume you are), you’re probably well aware of Gruber and his work as a writer, podcaster, friend of the site, and as a general tech person on the internet. Ahead of Apple’s big launch event coming up on September 9th, I thought it would be fun to feature the homescreen of one of the most well-known people in the Apple universe. [Image: The phone: iPhone 17 Pro, deep blue, 1 TB (of which only 200 GB is used, but that won’t stop me from wasting money on a 1 TB model this year too). The wallpaper: My wallpaper is a subtle gradient from very dark gray to black. For years I just stuck with a flat black wallpaper, as god and Steve Jobs intended. (You couldn’t change your homescreen wallpaper until iOS 4, and I remain unconvinced that was a good idea.) I like the subtle gradient now because it lets the dynamic island have a little visual contrast from the wallpaper background. The apps: I’ve currently got three todo/task apps on the homescreen, which I can’t recommend, but it’s currently working for me: Unforgetful, Finalist, and Due. (The red “1” badge on Unforgetful is for a reminder to send you this email and the screenshot of my homescreen.) I’ve also arguably got three notes apps, if you count Journal (in addition to Tot and Apple Notes). Mosaic is a TestFlight-only alternative to the official MLB app, which has a great story behind it. Rather than shutting it down, MLB hired its developer, Jason Weingardt, because Mosaic is so awesome. If I took the screenshot later tonight, you’d see a Live Activity from Mosaic of the Yankees game in the Dynamic Island. Kotoba is also TestFlight-only. It is, in my humble opinion, the best dictionary app for iOS, but because it uses the system-provided dictionaries and thesauruses to act as a dictionary app, it’s not permitted in the App Store. I look up words with it almost every single day. I wrote about it on Daring Fireball a while ago. The Siri app shows that I’m testing the iOS 27 betas. It’s good. I tend to use it side by side with ChatGPT for now, to compare responses, but going forward, I’ll use both. So having that alongside ChatGPT is in line with my having multiple todo apps and multiple note apps (and multiple messaging apps). I keep the badge on Mail counting my unread messages to remind myself that the heat death of the universe is inevitable. Oh, and my App Store app icon isn’t the actual App Store app, but instead a shortcut that jumps me right to the list of apps with pending updates to install. I also asked John to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back: * One show whose second season just finished: The Agency, on Paramount+. I think it’s probably the best spy series ever made. * One show whose sixth season is about to begin: Slow Horses, on Apple TV. I think it’s probably the most amusing spy series ever made. * Third, It’s Always Sunny in Philadelphia, whose 18th season just started; it’s the best and most realistic show set in Philadelphia ever made. Crowdsourced Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Bluesky. “Feels like this week is all Dolly Parton, Tim Curry, and now Transformers for Peter Cullen in terms of what people are watching and listening to!” — Carli “I’ve been playing A la Card and REALLY enjoying my time with it. It’s an indie roguelike deck builder game that feels like Slay the Spire and Balatro said ‘Let’s go out for food from a food truck.’ All cards can be mutated and changed via the events — their values, their effect, what triggers them. Great art and music, solid design, and it’s scratching an itch I didn’t know I had. Awesome game from a 2-person indie dev team.” — Tom “My preorder shipped early so I’ve been reading Emo Revival by Andrew Sacher and it’s a 10/10 so far.” — @thoughtlesskyle.bsky.social “Empire of AI, Karen Hao. Recently translated to PT-BR :)” — Milena “Tonight I’m going to finish House of Guinness. It’s a fine show but even better if you drink when watching it.” — Nick “I’ve been on a kick reading older sci-fi novels recently and came across Berserker by Fred Saberhagen (1967). Fantastic book but surprisingly hard to find a physical copy. Ended up purchasing an ePub. Highly recommend!” — Nathan Signing off I got a few good screentime reduction tips following last week’s issue. One person said they don’t install apps with an infinite scroll, which I thought was a good idea. They also have Screen Time enabled to block various things, but their partner holds the password to unlock Screen Time if needed. Clever! Another reader suggested zipping up their phone in a phone pocket. On my vacation next week, to make sure I actually unplug, I plan to deploy my favorite hack: hiding every gadget with a browser in my daughter’s closet. My only free time where I could potentially slip into mindless scrolling would be when she’s sleeping, but there’s no way I’m risking waking her up just to get out the laptop. More time for the important stuff — like playing Switch 2. See you in two weeks!

articles.title: Vivek Dahiya opens up about Divyanka Tripathi’s postpartum recovery after welcoming twins: says ‘It is real’
articles.summary: Popular television couple, Divyanka Tripathi and Vivek Dahiya recently welcomed twin baby boys and are enjoying parenthood. Recently, in an interview,.
articles.body: Popular television couple, Divyanka Tripathi and Vivek Dahiya recently welcomed twin baby boys and are enjoying parenthood. Recently, in an interview, Vivek spoke about how becoming parents has changed their lives. He also talked about postpartum depression and said it is very real.While talking to HindiRush, Vivek spoke about postpartum depression and explained that mothers experience many physical and hormonal changes after childbirth. He added that accepting these changes in their bodies can be one of the biggest challenges they face.He shared, “Postpartum depression is real. Because, you know, there are so many changes. There are hormonal changes. The mother starts realising, ‘My body is no longer the body I had before.’ You know, ‘I now have to live with this.’ And it is very difficult."Vivek further added how after giving birth to twin babies has affected Divyanka's core strength. He also revealed that the actress followed her workout routine regularly but adjusting to the sudden changes in her body was especially difficult for her. He said, "“Suddenly, it feels like jelly here. The core that you had is suddenly not there at all. You can’t even imagine life without your core, especially if you are someone who works out a lot. Your core is involved in everything. So suddenly, your core strength is gone.”The Yeh Hai Mohabbatein actor went on to talk about the uncertainty that comes with postpartum recovery, "On top of that, you have this jelly-like stomach. And you don’t know how you will get back, how you will bounce back, how long it will take. And your daily activity is just around feeding, feeding, feeding, feeding, feeding,” he said.In the interview, Vivek also spoke about the new phase of parenthood, "It’s a completely new phase, and there is a lot for us to learn. As parents, I feel the responsibility has increased because everything is new to us. I make mistakes and learn something new every day while trying to build a bond with my children. They were only three months old recently, so we have already come a long way. They are twins and were premature, so they were extremely tiny when we first held them. Their eyes would not even open properly. In the beginning, it was difficult to fully understand what was happening. But slowly, you realise that this child is now your responsibility for life, and they don’t know anything yet."Vivek described the parenthood phase as learning and beautiful, "For the last one-and-a-half years, I have been attending workshops on AI and learning how to train it by giving it the right prompts. I look at parenting in a similar way. Every day, I think about what I should say or do, what activities I should introduce and what a father should do to help them grow. Hopefully, they will turn out just fine. So, this is a beautiful phase, but it is also a phase of learning something new every day,” he shared.

articles.title: Dipika Kakar decorates house with flowers and lights for Eid-E-Milad; husband Shoaib Ibrahim celebrates Raksha Bandhan with sister Saba
articles.summary: Television couple, Dipika Kakar and husband Shoaib Ibrahim recently shared glimpses from the festival celebrations. The duo celebrated Eid-E-Milad and.
articles.body: Television couple, Dipika Kakar and husband Shoaib Ibrahim recently shared glimpses from the festival celebrations. The duo celebrated Eid-E-Milad and Raksha Bandhan with their family members and shared memorable moments in their latest vlogs. Dipika and Shoaib both shared vlogs on their respective YouTube channels where they were seen celebrating the festival and Dipika going for her infusion treatment for liver cancer.Dipika started her vlog by making special arrangements for Eid-E-Milad. She began the auspicious occasion by shopping. In the video, the Sasural Simar Ka actress was seen buying flowers to decorate her house. After decorating the house with lights and flowers, she showed the special arrangement. She beautifully decorated the house for Eid.Further in the video, Dipika and her son Ruhaan were seen preparing for prayers on the occasion of Eid. Ruhaan helped his mother lay out the mats and arrange the seating.Later, Dipika went for her infusion treatment. Dipika revealed that Shoaib finds it difficult to watch her get the injection and he doesn't stay back even for her blood tests. After getting discharged, she meets Ruhaan at a mall and plays with him.In Shoaib’s video, he began his day by preparing kheer early in the morning on the occasion of Eid-e-Milad. He later took his father for a medical checkup and gave his fans his health update. He later accompanied Dipika to the hospital for her infusion.In the evening, Shoaib's sister Saba Ibrahim and his niece Reza arrived to tie him rakhi. They tied rakhi around Shoaib's wrist and fed him sweets. Shoaib gave Saba and Reza an envelope with money.In one of his vlogs, Shoaib opened up about his plans to start a restaurant. He revealed that he has had this idea for a long time. He even shared that he did not want his restaurant to have an extensive menu. He stated that he wanted to serve a handful of dishes his family had been making at home for years. “My thought was that I want to open a restaurant, but I want to keep it very limited. I don’t want to have too many things on the menu,” he said.He also mentioned in the video that due to financial constraint, he has not been able to fulfill his dream but he plans to do it in the future. “A little bit of financial things have also been going up and down. You know what all has happened in the last two-four months. But Inshallah, we will do it. This is hot,” he said.
